title: Photons and the photoelectric effect; Wave–particle duality; Temperature, internal energy, thermal equilibrium; Specific heat capacity and latent heat; Gas laws and ideal gas equation
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: Q01-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; Q03-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; Q01-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; Q03-1#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: Q01-1#N.4b, Q03-1#N.4a, T01-1#N.2, T02-1#N.3a, T02-uk1#N.7, T05-1#N.2a, Q01-1#N.9a, Q03-1#N.17b, T01-1#N.5, T02-1#N.6, T02-uk1#N.10a, T05-1#N.6.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Threshold frequency
items.clue: Symbol f₀: below it a metal emits no electrons, however intense the light.

items.label: de Broglie wavelength
items.clue: The quantity h/p for any moving object; it gets shorter as momentum rises.

items.label: Electronvolt
items.clue: Energy unit equal to 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, convenient for single quanta of light.

items.label: Electron gun
items.clue: Hot filament plus an accelerating potential of a few kV, producing the beam.

questions.stem: Light with a wavelength of 500 nm in air passes from the air into water (n = 1.33). What is the energy of each photon while it travels through the water? Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and treat the speed of light in air as c.

An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 2.0 kV. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, m_e = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and treat the electron as non-relativistic. What is the de Broglie wavelength of the electron?

A 0.20 kg copper block at 80 °C is lowered into a large tank containing 200 kg of water at 20 °C. The water has far more internal energy than the block. Which statement describes the resultant thermal energy transfer?

options.text: From the block to the water, until they reach the same temperature.
From the water to the block, since the water has more internal energy.
Coldness passes from the water into the block, so the block cools down.
From the block to the water, until they have equal internal energies.

questions.stem: An electric kettle heats 250 g of water from 18 °C to 90 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4.18 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. How much energy is transferred to the water? Ignore energy transferred to the kettle and surroundings.

A student finds the specific latent heat of fusion of ice with a heater in a funnel of crushed ice, but sets up no control funnel. The room is warmer than 0 °C. How does her value compare with the true value?

options.text: Too high, because some of the heater's energy escapes to the room.
Too low, because ice melted by the room is counted as melted by the heater.
About right, because the ice stays at 0 °C, so it takes in no energy from the room.
Too low, because the meltwater cools the heater, so it supplies less energy.

questions.explanation: Specific latent heat = VIt ÷ mass melted. The room adds mass melted but nothing to VIt, so the value comes out low.

questions.stem: A cylinder contains 0.64 kg of oxygen gas, which consists of O₂ molecules. The molar mass of oxygen atoms is 16 g mol⁻¹, and N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. How many oxygen molecules are in the cylinder?
Predict first. Which observation from photoelectric experiments cannot be explained by the classical wave theory of light?

options.text: Photoelectrons are emitted without any measurable delay, even in very dim light.
More photoelectrons are emitted each second when the light is made much more intense.
More photoelectrons are emitted each second when the frequency of the light is raised.
Every photoelectron leaves the metal with kinetic energy exactly hf minus the work function.

questions.stem: A beam of electrons and a beam of protons are each accelerated from rest through 100 V and aimed at the same crystal, whose rows of atoms are 2.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m apart. Which beam shows clear diffraction?

options.text: Only the protons: they are heavier, so they hit the atoms harder and are scattered more.
Both equally: they have the same charge and the same p.d., so they gain the same energy.
Only the electrons: their wavelength is comparable with the spacing of the atoms.
Neither: diffraction is a property of waves, and both beams are made of particles.

questions.stem: Sample P is warmed from 10 °C to 30 °C. Sample Q is warmed from 290 K to 310 K. Which statement about the two temperature changes is correct?

options.text: P's rise of 20 °C is equivalent to a rise of 293 K.
The changes differ, since kelvins and °C differ in size.
Both undergo the same temperature change, 20 K.
P's rise is larger, since P's temperature tripled.

questions.stem: A 0.300 kg iron block at 80.0 °C is placed in 0.500 kg of water at 20.0 °C in an insulated container, and the block and the water reach a common temperature. The specific heat capacity of iron is 450 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, and the specific heat capacity of water is 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Energy transfer to the container and the surroundings is negligible. What is the common temperature?

A student measures the specific latent heat of vaporisation of water. A heater keeps water boiling in a beaker on a balance. At 50.0 W, the mass falls by 6.0 g in 600 s. At 80.0 W, it falls by 14.0 g in 600 s. The rate of energy loss to the surroundings is the same in both runs. What is the specific latent heat of vaporisation?
questions.explanation: The losses cancel: specific latent heat = (80.0 − 50.0) × 600 ÷ (0.0140 − 0.0060) = 18 000 ÷ 0.0080 = 2.25 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹.

questions.stem: Predict first. Students measure the pressure of three samples of gas, each sealed in a rigid container, at several temperatures between 0 °C and 100 °C. The samples are of different gases and different amounts, and each behaves as an ideal gas. For each sample they plot pressure against temperature in °C and get a straight line. They then extend each best-fit line to zero pressure. What do they find?

options.text: All three lines reach zero pressure at the same temperature, 0 °C.
All three lines reach zero pressure at the same temperature, about −273 °C.
The steepest line reaches zero pressure at the highest temperature.
Each line reaches zero pressure at a temperature set by its kind of gas.
